title: Lime rolls out its in-house “Lime Vision” camera AI, which alerts scooter riders on sidewalks, to half of its Seattle fleet of about 7,000 scooters by 1 June 2026
summary: Lime Vision, Lime's in-house camera AI, detects sidewalk riding and sounds repeating alerts; Seattle's transport department reported its rollout on 9 June 2026 without outcome data.
account: Nicholas Deshais of The Seattle Times reported on 20 March 2026 that Lime would fit “Lime Vision” to its Seattle scooters. The Spokesman-Review syndicated the report. Lime Vision is a system of cameras and AI software that Lime developed in-house to detect sidewalk riding. It emits audible alerts that repeat until the scooter leaves the sidewalk or the trip ends. Lime would fit it to about 3,500 vehicles, half its Seattle fleet, by 1 June 2026, and to the whole fleet by year's end. New and retrofitted scooters were to arrive from mid-April. Parker Dawson, Lime's regional government relations lead, said that the technology had been tested in Seattle in recent months. He said that Seattle would get it before any other city. He said that it coaches riders and does not slow the scooter. He would not say why the scooters do not slow down on sidewalks as they do under geofencing at Seattle Center. Jon Scholes of the Downtown Seattle Association called sidewalk riding a safety issue. Lime shares data with a dashboard of the Seattle Department of Transportation. The article gives no figures on sidewalk riding or complaints before or after deployment. Permits that the department updated on 1 April 2026 require scooter companies to detect sidewalk riding on at least half the standing fleet within the second quarter of 2026 and on all devices by the end of 2026. The department described these permits on 14 May 2026. It said that it could add fines or account suspension once testing confirms that the sensors work as intended. On 9 June 2026 the department wrote that Lime was rolling out AI detection of sidewalk riding with audible alerts. Neither post gives figures on sidewalk riding.

fields.account: Nicholas Deshais of The Seattle Times reported on 20 March 2026 that Lime would fit “Lime Vision” to its Seattle scooters. The Spokesman-Review syndicated the report. Lime Vision is a system of cameras and AI software that Lime developed in-house to detect sidewalk riding. It emits audible alerts that repeat until the scooter leaves the sidewalk or the trip ends. Lime would fit it to about 3,500 vehicles, half its Seattle fleet, by 1 June 2026, and to the whole fleet by year's end. New and retrofitted scooters were to arrive from mid-April. Parker Dawson, Lime's regional government relations lead, said that the technology had been tested in Seattle in recent months. He said that Seattle would get it before any other city. He said that it coaches riders and does not slow the scooter. He would not say why the scooters do not slow down on sidewalks as they do under geofencing at Seattle Center. Jon Scholes of the Downtown Seattle Association called sidewalk riding a safety issue. Lime shares data with a dashboard of the Seattle Department of Transportation. The article gives no figures on sidewalk riding or complaints before or after deployment. Permits that the department updated on 1 April 2026 require scooter companies to detect sidewalk riding on at least half the standing fleet within the second quarter of 2026 and on all devices by the end of 2026. The department described these permits on 14 May 2026. It said that it could add fines or account suspension once testing confirms that the sensors work as intended. On 9 June 2026 the department wrote that Lime was rolling out AI detection of sidewalk riding with audible alerts. Neither post gives figures on sidewalk riding.
